title: UNIT 8: PROBABILITY
notes:
✓ Probability → a measure of how likely an event is to occur.

✓ Probability is always between 0 and 1:
◆ P(E) = 0 → impossible
◆ 0 < P(E) < 1 → possible
◆ P(E) = 1 → certain

✓ For equally likely outcomes:
P(E) = Number of favorable outcomes ÷ Total number of possible outcomes.

title: RANDOM EXPERIMENTS & OUTCOMES
notes:
✓ Random experiment → an experiment whose exact outcome cannot be predicted with certainty before it is performed.

◆ Examples → tossing a coin, rolling a die, or selecting a card.

✓ Outcome → a possible result of a random experiment.

✓ Sample space (S) → the set of all possible outcomes.

Example:
◆ Coin toss → S = {H, T}
◆ Die roll → S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}.

title: EVENTS
notes:
✓ Event → a collection of one or more outcomes from a sample space.

Example: When a die is rolled:
A = getting an even number = {2, 4, 6}.

✓ Simple event → contains only one outcome.
Example → getting 4.

✓ Compound event → contains two or more outcomes.
Example → getting an even number.

title: TYPES OF EVENTS
notes:
◆ Simple event → has exactly one outcome.
Example → rolling a 5.

◆ Compound event → has more than one outcome.
Example → rolling an even number.

◆ Certain event → must occur; P(E) = 1.
Example → rolling a number less than 7 on a standard die.

◆ Impossible event → cannot occur; P(E) = 0.
Example → rolling 8 on a standard die.

◆ Mutually exclusive events → cannot occur at the same time.
Example → getting an odd number and an even number in one die roll.

◆ Exhaustive events → a group of events that together contain all possible outcomes.

◆ Complementary events → an event and its complement; exactly one occurs.
Example → getting a 6 and not getting a 6.

title: PROBABILITY OF AN EVENT
notes:
✓ If all outcomes are equally likely:

P(A) = n(A) ÷ n(S)

✓ Where:
◆ P(A) → probability of event A
◆ n(A) → number of favorable outcomes
◆ n(S) → total number of outcomes

Example:
A die is rolled. Find the probability of getting an even number.

Favorable outcomes = {2,4,6} = 3
Total outcomes = 6
P(A) = 3/6 = 1/2.

title: COMPLEMENT OF AN EVENT
notes:
✓ Complement of A (A′) → the event that A does not occur.

✓ Formula:
P(A′) = 1 − P(A)

Therefore:
P(A) + P(A′) = 1

Example:
If P(rain) = 0.3,
P(no rain) = 1 − 0.3 = 0.7.

title: FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLE OF COUNTING
notes:
✓ If one task can be completed in m ways and another task can be completed in n ways, then both tasks can be completed in:

m × n ways.

✓ General rule:
Total ways = n₁ × n₂ × n₃ × ...

Example:
There are 3 shirts and 2 trousers.
Number of outfits = 3 × 2 = 6.

✓ Use multiplication when choices occur in stages.

title: FACTORIAL
notes:
✓ Factorial of a positive integer n is:

n! = n(n−1)(n−2)...3×2×1

✓ Special case:
0! = 1

Examples:
5! = 5×4×3×2×1 = 120
4! = 24
3! = 6

✓ Factorials are important in permutations and combinations.

title: PERMUTATION
notes:
✓ Permutation → an arrangement of objects where ORDER MATTERS.

✓ Formula:
nPr = n! ÷ (n−r)!

Example:
Arrange 3 students selected from 5 students:
5P3 = 5! ÷ 2! = 60.

✓ Key idea → permutation = arrangement and order matters.

title: PERMUTATION OF ALL OBJECTS
notes:
✓ When all n distinct objects are arranged in a row:

Number of arrangements = n!

Example:
4 students can be arranged in:
4! = 4×3×2×1 = 24 ways.

✓ If changing the order creates a different arrangement, permutation is used.

title: CIRCULAR PERMUTATION
notes:
✓ Circular permutation → arranging objects around a circle.

✓ For n distinct objects arranged around a circle:
Number of arrangements = (n−1)!

Example:
4 people sitting around a round table:
(4−1)! = 3! = 6 arrangements.

In a circle, rotations of the same arrangement are considered identical.

◆ Linear arrangement → n!
◆ Circular arrangement → (n−1)!.

title: COMBINATION
notes:
✓ Combination → selecting objects where ORDER DOES NOT MATTER.

✓ Formula:
nCr = n! ÷ [r!(n−r)!]

Example:
Select 2 students from 5 students:
5C2 = 5! ÷ (2!×3!) = 10.

✓ Key idea → combination = selection; order does not matter.

title: PERMUTATION vs COMBINATION
notes:
✓ Permutation → order matters.
Example → awarding 1st, 2nd and 3rd places.

✓ Combination → order does not matter.
Example → selecting 3 students for a team.

✓ Quick rule:
◆ Arrangement/order → nPr
◆ Selection/group → nCr

✓ Relationship:
nPr = nCr × r!

title: BINOMIAL THEOREM
notes:
✓ Binomial theorem → a method for expanding a binomial raised to a positive integer power.

✓ Formula:
(a+b)ⁿ = Σ[nCr × aⁿ⁻ʳ × bʳ], where r = 0 to n.

Expanded form:
(a+b)ⁿ = nC0aⁿ + nC1aⁿ⁻¹b + nC2aⁿ⁻²b² + ... + nCnbⁿ.

✓ The coefficients are obtained from combinations or Pascal's triangle.

title: BINOMIAL THEOREM EXAMPLE
notes:
Example: Expand (x + 2)³.

Using:
(a+b)³ = a³ + 3a²b + 3ab² + b³

Therefore:
(x+2)³ = x³ + 6x² + 12x + 8.

✓ Pascal's triangle gives the coefficients:
1
1 1
1 2 1
1 3 3 1
1 4 6 4 1.

title: ADDITION RULE OF PROBABILITY
notes:
✓ For two events A and B:

P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)

✓ Where:
◆ A ∪ B → A or B occurs
◆ A ∩ B → both A and B occur

✓ If A and B are mutually exclusive:
P(A ∩ B) = 0

Therefore:
P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B).

title: PROBABILITY USING COUNTING
notes:
✓ Counting techniques can be used to calculate probability.

✓ Steps:
◆ Find the total number of possible outcomes.
◆ Find the number of favorable outcomes.
◆ Use P(A) = favorable outcomes ÷ total outcomes.

Example:
From 5 students, 2 are selected.
Total selections = 5C2 = 10.
If one particular pair is required, favorable selections = 1.

P(A) = 1/10.

title: UNIT 8 QUICK FORMULA SUMMARY
notes:
✓ Probability:
P(A) = n(A)/n(S)

✓ Complement:
P(A′) = 1 − P(A)

✓ Counting principle:
Total ways = n₁ × n₂ × n₃ × ...

✓ Factorial:
n! = n(n−1)...2×1
0! = 1

✓ Permutation:
nPr = n!/(n−r)!

✓ Circular permutation:
(n−1)!

✓ Combination:
nCr = n!/[r!(n−r)!]

✓ Addition rule:
P(A∪B) = P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B)

✓ Binomial theorem:
(a+b)ⁿ = Σ[nCr aⁿ⁻ʳbʳ].
